metadata.title: Mobility-as-a-Service Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how a mobility platform would need to change when public transport must work for days without connectivity, a city reallocates curb space overnight, a payment acquirer exits the market, or an evacuation combines offline travel, emergency curb rules, and unsettled money.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A city or operator configures parking spaces, permits, fares, and payment rules centrally; a driver or passenger starts a session or taps a validator; the platform authorizes payment through a configured provider; and transactions are settled and reported to the operator. The design assumes the network is reachable, curb use is stable during a booking, and the selected payment and settlement path remains available.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design separates mobility intent, entitlement, session, physical place or transit leg, effective policy, capacity allocation, local device decision, payment instruction, tender, acquirer, authorization, operator receivable, platform fee, ledger entry, settlement route, and synchronization result. Policies and value can move independently, so devices operate within bounded offline authority, curb rights can be reallocated with explicit displacement, and an acquirer can be replaced without losing the journey or operator balance.
metadata.note: These tests begin with public-service obligations, emergency use of city space, and payment-market concentration. The change is more than offline caching: mobility rights, physical capacity, payment acceptance, and settlement are modeled separately so each can change without invalidating the others.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: A national resilience rule requires transit and essential parking to work through a 72-hour network isolation
stressors.detection: Final resilience requirements, operator service tiers, validator and meter inventories, local policy and key freshness, connectivity state, offline transaction volume, device storage, reconciliation tests, abuse signals, and passenger support reports.
stressors.attractor: Central authorization, current fare or parking policy, account lookup, and payment approval are unavailable while people still need to travel. Rejecting everyone stops an essential service; accepting unlimited local claims creates fraud, duplicate sessions, stale rules, and settlement uncertainty when connectivity returns.
stressors.businessReaction: Define which journeys and users must continue, distribute signed policy and bounded local authority, show clear offline terms, record tamper-evident events, cap exposure, support inspectors and staff, restore connectivity in waves, reconcile conflicts, and settle operators without charging riders twice.
stressors.residue: Separate travel or parking entitlement, policy version, device, locally trusted credential, offline authority, session event, fare calculation, payment promise, risk limit, synchronization attempt, conflict, final charge, operator receivable, and rider adjustment. A device decides within explicit time and value bounds and later reconciliation preserves both local and central histories.

impacts.effect: Fare modernization includes continuity for essential travel when central services and networks are unavailable.
Transit leaders can modernize collection without making network reachability a prerequisite for boarding.
Operations can see policy freshness, offline authority, exposure, storage, synchronization, and rider correction by device.
Tap success distinguishes safe offline acceptance, online authorization, deferred reconciliation, and final correction.
Adds signed offline policy, bounded device authorization, local journey evidence, staged reconciliation, and rider redress.
Keeps boarding fast while making offline acceptance limits and later financial treatment explicit.
Versions fare rules and produces deterministic calculations from offline and online journey events.
Manages device trust, policy freshness, local limits, storage, health, and reconciliation state.
Preserves ordered local and central events with idempotent replay and visible conflict resolution.
Owns offline service continuity with fare, payments, operator control, device vendors, security, support, and settlement teams.
Makes multi-day offline open-payment continuity a transit-platform benchmark.

stressors.name: A city reallocates thousands of paid curb spaces to emergency transit and relief use overnight
stressors.detection: Emergency declaration, geospatial curb inventory, effective policy orders, active reservations and permits, occupancy and access state, transit and relief routes, signage and field deployment, citizen communications, and enforcement readiness.
stressors.attractor: A parking space sold or permitted yesterday becomes a bus lane, staging area, accessible pickup point, or prohibited zone today. Static zone configuration continues selling unavailable inventory, access systems admit vehicles, enforcement penalizes yesterday's valid users, and operators cannot explain displaced revenue or service.
stressors.businessReaction: Publish the emergency curb plan, stop incompatible sales and entry, protect critical users, identify every affected reservation and permit, offer relocation or refund, update devices and enforcement, communicate locally, monitor compliance and congestion, and restore or redesign uses as conditions change.
stressors.residue: Separate physical curb segment, use right, policy version, effective interval, authority, eligibility, capacity allocation, reservation, permit, access decision, enforcement rule, displacement, alternative, refund, signage, and observed outcome. Changing curb purpose invalidates only conflicting rights and creates an explicit migration path for affected users.

impacts.effect: Parking operations become a governed allocation of city space that can change safely during an emergency.
Parking directors can change curb purpose while coordinating inventory, access, payment, enforcement, and customer remedy.
Configuration carries authority, effective time, priority, conflicting rights, migration, signage, and field-readiness state.
Occupancy balance reflects the current intended use of each curb segment rather than historical parking supply.
Adds emergency policy activation, affected-right discovery, relocation, refund, device rollout, and enforcement readiness.
Enforcement evaluates the rule that was effective for the place, user, and time and recognizes displaced valid rights.
Versions curb uses and rule precedence with authority, geography, eligibility, and effective intervals.
Finds conflicting reservations and permits and records relocation, cancellation, priority, and refund.
Distributes current rules and protects previously valid users during the policy transition.
Owns curb reallocation with city policy, transit, emergency services, access, enforcement, field operations, finance, and communications.
Makes rapid multi-use curb reconfiguration and fair user recovery a full-stack mobility benchmark.

stressors.name: A dominant payment acquirer exits several markets and freezes unsettled mobility funds
stressors.detection: Acquirer and regulator notices, contract and market coverage, authorization routes, token portability, transaction and chargeback state, operator receivables, merchant balances, reserves, settlement files, treasury exposure, and partner support cases.
stressors.attractor: Journeys were completed and operators expect revenue, but authorization tokens, merchant accounts, fees, reserves, disputes, and settlement are bound to a provider that can no longer process or release funds. Switching checkout routing does not explain old balances or prevent riders and cities from being charged again.
stressors.businessReaction: Stop unsafe routing, quantify funds and markets exposed, preserve operator receivables, activate alternative acceptance, migrate eligible tokens and merchants, communicate service limits, reconcile every completed journey, pursue recovery, and settle partners through a governed replacement path.
stressors.residue: Separate mobility session, payment instruction, payment method reference, merchant, acquirer, authorization, capture, fee, reserve, chargeback, operator receivable, platform receivable, ledger posting, settlement obligation, settlement route, bank movement, and recovery claim. New transactions can change providers while old economic rights remain traceable.

impacts.effect: Partner economics remain understandable when payment acceptance and movement of funds switch providers.
Partners integrate once while market-specific payment and settlement routes can be replaced beneath the contract.
Reporting separates journey value, provider fees, unsettled exposure, recovery, operator payment, and platform margin.
Transaction success ends with correct economic posting and settlement treatment, not only initial authorization.
Adds provider routing, market migration, merchant portability, frozen-fund exposure, claims, and partner reconciliation.
Keeps operator and mobility partners stable while payment-market adapters and settlement routes change.
Routes acceptance by market, method, service, provider health, legal scope, and migration state.
Preserves double-entry obligations and independently routes settlement, recovery, adjustment, and partner payout.
Versions provider capability, certification, market coverage, commercial terms, suspension, and replacement.
Owns economic continuity with treasury, payment providers, operators, partner success, finance, risk, legal, and support.
Makes provider-independent municipal and transit settlement a mobility-payments benchmark.

stressors.name: A regional evacuation begins during network isolation after the payment acquirer freezes funds
stressors.detection: Emergency orders and routes, effective curb and fare policies, device connectivity and policy freshness, local capacity, offline sessions, payment-route health, operator balances, displaced reservations, field status, and public communications.
stressors.attractor: People need immediate transit, parking, pickup, and relief access; familiar curb space changes purpose; validators and meters cannot reach central services; and the primary payment route cannot move money. A central online purchase flow would reject essential journeys or create untraceable promises and duplicate recovery later.
stressors.businessReaction: Activate emergency mobility policy, reallocate curb and capacity, distribute bounded free or deferred entitlements, keep devices operating offline, communicate routes and terms, prioritize vulnerable users, reconcile journeys after restoration, and settle operators through alternative or public funding without double charging.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: effective-dated curb policy reallocates physical capacity, bounded offline authority preserves essential sessions, and provider-independent ledger obligations retain economic truth until a valid settlement route becomes available. One emergency workflow coordinates the existing parts.

impacts.effect: City policy can turn the existing mobility network into an emergency public service without losing fairness or accountability.
Policy leaders coordinate current capacity, emergency rights, offline service, and eventual economic treatment.
The emergency view tracks policy activation, capacity, access, displacement, service reach, device exposure, and settlement backlog.
The decision cycle measures time from emergency fact to executable policy across streets, devices, partners, and communications.
Composes emergency zones, mobility capacity, offline service state, user impact, and recovery outcomes for city control.
Reuses existing policy, offline, and ledger residues to test and activate the evacuation plan.
Provides the current spatial view of demand, capacity, affected populations, service state, and outcomes.
Coordinates policy approval, field changes, device rollout, exceptions, reconciliation, and restoration.
Sends location- and audience-specific emergency access, displacement, service, and recovery information.
Coordinates emergency policy with parking, transit, payment, partner, field, data, accessibility, finance, and public-information teams.
Makes cross-mode emergency policy and service communication a MaaS benchmark.
